Rule.title: Ensure accounts in /etc/passwd use shadowed passwords
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Local accounts can use shadowed passwords. With shadowed passwords, the passwords are saved in the shadow password file, /etc/shadow, encrypted by a salted one-way hash. Accounts with a shadowed password have an x in the second field in /etc/passwd.

Rationale:
The /etc/passwd file also contains information like user ID's and group ID's that are used by many system programs. Therefore, the /etc/passwd file must remain world readable. In spite of encoding the password with a randomly-generated one-way hash function, an attacker could still break the system if they got access to the /etc/passwd file. This can be mitigated by using shadowed passwords, thus moving the passwords in the /etc/passwd file to /etc/shadow. The /etc/shadow file is set so only root will be able to read and write. This helps mitigate the risk of an attacker gaining access to the encoded passwords with which to perform a dictionary attack.
Note:
• All accounts must have passwords or be locked to prevent the account from being used by an unauthorized user.
• A user account with an empty second field in /etc/passwd allows the account to be logged into by providing only the username.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to set accounts to use shadowed passwords and migrate passwords in /etc/passwd to /etc/shadow:
# pwconv
Investigate to determine if the account is logged in and what it is being used for, to determine if it needs to be forced off.
Internal Only - General

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify that no output is returned:
# awk -F: '($2 != "x" ) { print "User: \"" $1 "\" is not set to shadowed
passwords"}' /etc/passwd

Rule.title: Ensure /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>An account with an empty password field means that anybody may log in as that user without providing a password.

Rationale:
All accounts must have passwords or be locked to prevent the account from being used by an unauthorized user.</VulnDiscussion>

If any accounts in the /etc/shadow file do not have a password, run the following command to lock the account until it can be determined why it does not have a password:
# passwd -l <username>
Also, check to see if the account is logged in and investigate what it is being used for to determine if it needs to be forced off.

Run the following command and verify that no output is returned:

Rationale:
Groups defined in the /etc/passwd file but not in the /etc/group file pose a threat to system security since group permissions are not properly managed.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.description:

Rationale:
Any users assigned to the shadow group would be granted read access to the /etc/shadow file. If attackers can gain read access to the /etc/shadow file, they can easily run a password cracking program against the hashed passwords to break them.
Other security information that is stored in the /etc/shadow file (such as expiration) could also be useful to subvert additional user accounts.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate UIDs exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate User ID (UID), it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/passwd file and change the UID field.

Rationale:
Users must be assigned unique UIDs for accountability and to ensure appropriate access protections.
Satisfies: SRG-OS-000104-GPOS-00051, SRG-OS-000121-GPOS-00062, SRG-OS- 000042-GPOS-00020</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique UIDs and review all files owned by the shared UIDs to determine which UID they are supposed to belong to.

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate GIDs exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the groupadd program will not let you create a duplicate Group ID (GID), it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/group file and change the GID field.

Rationale:
User groups must be assigned unique GIDs for accountability and to ensure appropriate access protections.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique GIDs and review all files owned by the shared GID to determine which group they are supposed to belong to.

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate user names exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate user name, it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/passwd file and change the user name.

Rationale:
If a user is assigned a duplicate user name, it will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has a UID of 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has a UID of 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. Effectively, the UID is shared, which is a security problem.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content: Based on the results of the audit script, establish unique user names for the users. File ownerships will automatically reflect the change as long as the users have unique UIDs.

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate group names exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the groupadd program will not let you create a duplicate group name, it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/group file and change the group name.

Rationale:
If a group is assigned a duplicate group name, it will create and have access to files with the first GID for that group in /etc/group. Effectively, the GID is shared, which is a security problem.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure local interactive user home directories are configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The user home directory is space defined for the particular user to set local environment variables and to store personal files. While the system administrator can establish secure permissions for users' home directories, the users can easily override these.
Users can be defined in /etc/passwd without a home directory or with a home directory that does not actually exist.

Rationale:
Since the user is accountable for files stored in the user home directory, the user must be the owner of the directory. Group or world-writable user home directories may enable malicious users to steal or modify other users' data or to gain another user's system privileges. If the user's home directory does not exist or is unassigned, the user will be placed in "/" and will not be able to write any files or have local environment variables set.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
If a local interactive users' home directory is undefined and/or doesn't exist, follow local site policy and perform one of the following:
• Lock the user account
• Remove the user from the system
• Create a directory for the user. If undefined, edit /etc/passwd and add the absolute path to the directory to the last field of the user.

Rule.title: Ensure local interactive user dot directories access is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>While the system administrator can establish secure permissions for users' "dot" directories, the users can easily override these. Dot directories are the hidden subdirectories within a user's home directory (their names begin with a.) that hold per- user configuration, state, and credential material. Common examples include:
•.ssh — holds the user's SSH private keys, authorized_keys, known_hosts, and client configuration. Read or write access by other users can lead to credential theft or unauthorized authentication.
•.gnupg — holds the user's GnuPG keyring and trust database.
•.config,.local — hold application configuration and per-user data (XDG base directories).
•.cache — holds cached application data, which can include tokens or session material.

Rationale:
User configuration directories with excessive or incorrect access may enable malicious users to read, steal, or modify other users' data — or to gain another user's system privileges. A weakly-permissioned.ssh directory is particularly dangerous: if it is group- or world-writable, another user can drop an authorized_keys entry and obtain the victim's identity; if it is readable by others, private key material can be exfiltrated.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Making global modifications to users' directories without alerting the user community can result in unexpected outages and unhappy users. Therefore, it is recommended that a monitoring policy be established to report user dot directory permissions and determine the action to be taken in accordance with site policy.
The following script will, within local interactive users' home directories:
• remove excessive permissions on dot directories (max 0750;.ssh max 0700)
• change ownership of dot directories to the user
• change group ownership of dot directories to the user's primary group Note: Like the audit, this remediation scopes its action to local interactive users' home directories only and does not traverse the entire filesystem.

{
l_maxsize="1000" # Maximum number of local interactive users before
warning (Default 1,000)
l_valid_shells="^($( awk -F\/ '$NF != "nologin" {print}' /etc/shells | sed
-rn '/^\//{s,/,\\\\/,g;p}' | paste -s -d '|' - ))$"
a_user_and_home=() # Create array with local users and their home
directories
while read -r l_local_user l_local_user_home; do # Populate array with
users and user home location
[[ -n "$l_local_user" && -n "$l_local_user_home" ]] &&
a_user_and_home+=("$l_local_user:$l_local_user_home")
done <<< "$(awk -v pat="$l_valid_shells" -F: '$(NF) ~ pat { print $1 " "
$(NF-1) }' /etc/passwd)"
l_asize="${#a_user_and_home[@]}" # Here if we want to look at number of
users before proceeding
[ "${#a_user_and_home[@]}" -gt "$l_maxsize" ] && printf '%s\n' "" " **
INFO **" \
" - \"$l_asize\" Local interactive users found on the system" \
" - This may be a long running check" ""
dir_access_fix()
{
l_max="$( printf '%o' $(( 0777 & ~$l_mask)) )"
if [ $(( $l_mode & $l_mask )) -gt 0 ]; then
printf '%s\n' "" " - Directory: \"$l_hddir\" is mode: \"$l_mode\"
and should be mode: \"$l_max\" or more restrictive" \
" Updating directory: \"$l_hddir\" to be mode: \"$l_max\" or
more restrictive"
chmod "$l_change" "$l_hddir"
fi
if [[ ! "$l_owner" =~ ($l_user) ]]; then
printf '%s\n' "" " - Directory: \"$l_hddir\" owned by: \"$l_owner\"
and should be owned by \"${l_user//|/ or }\"" \
" Updating directory: \"$l_hddir\" to be owned by \"${l_user//|/
or }\""
chown "$l_user" "$l_hddir"
fi
if [[ ! "$l_gowner" =~ ($l_group) ]]; then
printf '%s\n' "" " - Directory: \"$l_hddir\" group owned by:
\"$l_gowner\" and should be group owned by \"${l_group//|/ or }\"" \
" Updating directory: \"$l_hddir\" to be group owned by
\"${l_group//|/ or }\""
chgrp "$l_group" "$l_hddir"
fi
}
while IFS=: read -r l_user l_home; do
# Skip home directories that reside on a network / remote filesystem
l_fstype="$(findmnt -no FSTYPE --target "$l_home" 2>/dev/null)"
case "$l_fstype" in
nfs|nfs4|cifs|smbfs|smb3|fuse.sshfs|afs|ncpfs|glusterfs|ceph)
printf '%s\n' "" " - User: \"$l_user\" Home Directory:
\"$l_home\" skipped (remote/network filesystem: $l_fstype)"
continue ;;
esac
if [ -d "$l_home" ]; then
l_group="$(id -gn "$l_user" | xargs)";l_group="${l_group// /|}"
Internal Only - General
while IFS= read -r -d $'\0' l_hddir; do
while read -r l_mode l_owner l_gowner; do
case "$(basename "$l_hddir")" in
.ssh )
l_mask='0077'; l_change="g-rwx,o-rwx"; dir_access_fix ;;
* )
l_mask='0027'; l_change="g-w,o-rwx"; dir_access_fix ;;
esac
done < <(stat -Lc '%#a %U %G' "$l_hddir")
done < <(find "$l_home" -xdev -type d -name '.*' -print0)
fi
done <<< "$(printf '%s\n' "${a_user_and_home[@]}")"

Note: This recommendation intentionally avoids a full-filesystem traversal ( find /) when locating dot directories. A system-wide search for. -prefixed directories is expensive and can take a very long time on hosts with large or networked filesystems, and it would repeatedly cross into directory trees (caches, build artifacts, application data) that are not user credential stores. Instead, the audit and remediation are scoped to the home directories of local interactive users — users who have a valid login shell as enumerated from /etc/passwd and /etc/shells — and use find "$l_home" -xdev -type d -name '.*' (the -xdev guard also keeps the scan on the home filesystem and prevents descent into mounted filesystems). This mirrors the scope of recommendation 7.2.10.
Limitation of this scope: Dot directories that hold sensitive material but reside outside local interactive users' home directories — for example, credential or configuration directories created under /opt, /srv, application working directories, or the home directories of service/system accounts that use nologin / false shells — are not evaluated by this automated check. Administrators should ensure, through separate review or site-specific tooling, that no unexpected dot directories with weak permissions (group- or world-writable, or readable by other where they hold secrets) exist outside the audited scope. If your environment stores per-user credentials outside standard interactive home directories, treat those locations under a separate control.

[ "${#a_user_and_home[@]}" -gt "$l_maxsize" ] && printf '%s\n' "" " **
INFO **" \
" - \"$l_asize\" Local interactive users found on the system" \
" - This may be a long running check" ""
dir_access_chk()
{
a_access_out=()
l_max="$( printf '%o' $(( 0777 & ~$l_mask)) )"
if [ $(( $l_mode & $l_mask )) -gt 0 ]; then
a_access_out+=(" - Directory: \"$l_hddir\" is mode: \"$l_mode\" and
should be mode: \"$l_max\" or more restrictive")
fi
if [[ ! "$l_owner" =~ ($l_user) ]]; then
a_access_out+=(" - Directory: \"$l_hddir\" owned by: \"$l_owner\"
and should be owned by \"${l_user//|/ or }\"")
fi
if [[ ! "$l_gowner" =~ ($l_group) ]]; then
a_access_out+=(" - Directory: \"$l_hddir\" group owned by:
\"$l_gowner\" and should be group owned by \"${l_group//|/ or }\"")
fi
}
while IFS=: read -r l_user l_home; do
a_hddirout=()
# Skip home directories that reside on a network / remote filesystem
l_fstype="$(findmnt -no FSTYPE --target "$l_home" 2>/dev/null)"
case "$l_fstype" in
nfs|nfs4|cifs|smbfs|smb3|fuse.sshfs|afs|ncpfs|glusterfs|ceph)
printf '%s\n' "" " - User: \"$l_user\" Home Directory:
\"$l_home\" skipped (remote/network filesystem: $l_fstype)"
continue ;;
esac
if [ -d "$l_home" ]; then
l_group="$(id -gn "$l_user" | xargs)";l_group="${l_group// /|}"
while IFS= read -r -d $'\0' l_hddir; do
while read -r l_mode l_owner l_gowner; do
case "$(basename "$l_hddir")" in
.ssh )
l_mask='0077'; dir_access_chk
Internal Only - General
[ "${#a_access_out[@]}" -gt 0 ] &&
a_hddirout+=("${a_access_out[@]}") ;;
* )
l_mask='0027'; dir_access_chk
[ "${#a_access_out[@]}" -gt 0 ] &&
a_hddirout+=("${a_access_out[@]}") ;;
esac
done < <(stat -Lc '%#a %U %G' "$l_hddir")
done < <(find "$l_home" -xdev -type d -name '.*' -print0)
fi
if [ "${#a_hddirout[@]}" -gt 0 ]; then
a_output2+=(" - User: \"$l_user\" Home Directory: \"$l_home\""
"${a_hddirout[@]}")
fi
done <<< "$(printf '%s\n' "${a_user_and_home[@]}")"
if [ "${#a_output2[@]}" -le 0 ]; then # If a_output2 is empty, we pass
printf '%s\n' "- Audit Result:" " ** PASS **"
else
printf '%s\n' "- Audit Result:" " ** FAIL **" " - * Reasons for audit
failure * :" "${a_output2[@]}" ""
fi
}
